intro.title: Find your best-fit platform
intro.text: There is no single best automation tool, only the best fit for your team, apps, volume, and data. Answer seven quick questions and we will show your top match and runner-up.
bullets: Covers Zapier, Make, n8n, Power Automate, and custom builds
Weighs skills, apps, volume, complexity, and data sensitivity

zapier.name: Zapier
zapier.text: The easiest place to start, with the largest library of app integrations. Best for simple, linear workflows built by non-technical teams. Costs can climb as volume grows, so keep an eye on task usage.

make.name: Make
make.text: A visual builder that handles branching, data mapping, and higher volumes affordably. A strong fit for a tech-comfortable person who wants more control than Zapier without writing code.

n8n.name: n8n
n8n.text: Source-available and very flexible, with a self-hosted option that keeps data on your own servers and keeps costs low at high volume. Best with a developer or technical person to set it up and maintain it.

power.name: Microsoft Power Automate
power.text: The natural choice if your business runs on Microsoft 365. Works closely with Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Excel, and some capabilities may already be included in your Microsoft licenses.

custom.name: A done-for-you or custom build
custom.text: When workflows are complex, data is sensitive, or nobody has time to build and maintain them, a partner can design, build, and support the system on whichever platform fits, with custom code where needed.

How the picker scores your answers

Each answer adds points to the platforms that suit it. Your result shows the platform with the highest share of its possible points, plus the runner-up, so you can see how close the call is.
faq: Which is better, Zapier or Make?

Zapier is easier to learn and connects to more apps out of the box. Make offers more control over branching and data, and is usually more economical at higher volumes. Non-technical teams often start with Zapier; tech-comfortable builders often prefer Make.

n8n is source-available and can be self-hosted, which avoids per-run fees but means paying for and maintaining a server. It also offers a paid cloud version. Check the current license and pricing on n8n's site.
Yes, though workflows must be rebuilt, since platforms do not share a format. Documenting each workflow's trigger, steps, and data makes switching far easier.
